sets.title: Dulce et Decorum Est
sets.author: Wilfred Owen
sets.source: Dulce et Decorum Est, in Poems (ed. Siegfried Sassoon), Chatto & Windus, 1920 (written 1917)
sets.headnote: Wilfred Owen was a British infantry officer who served on the Western Front and was killed in November 1918. He drafted this poem in 1917 after being treated for shell shock; it was published after his death. The Latin title and closing words come from the Roman poet Horace: it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country.
sets.body:
Bent double, like old beggars under sacks,
Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge,
Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs
And towards our distant rest began to trudge.
Men marched asleep. Many had lost their boots
But limped on, blood-shod. All went lame; all blind;
Drunk with fatigue; deaf even to the hoots
Of tired, outstripped Five-Nines that dropped behind.

Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!—An ecstasy of fumbling,
Fitting the clumsy helmets just in time;
But someone still was yelling out and stumbling,
And flound'ring like a man in fire or lime...
Dim, through the misty panes and thick green light,
As under a green sea, I saw him drowning.

In all my dreams, before my helpless sight,
He plunges at me, guttering, choking, drowning.

If in some smothering dreams you too could pace
Behind the wagon that we flung him in,
And watch the white eyes writhing in his face,
His hanging face, like a devil's sick of sin;
If you could hear, at every jolt, the blood
Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs,
Obscene as cancer, bitter as the cud
Of vile, incurable sores on innocent tongues,—
My friend, you would not tell with such high zest
To children ardent for some desperate glory,
The old Lie: Dulce et decorum est
Pro patria mori.

pair.title: The Soldier
pair.author: Rupert Brooke
pair.source: The Soldier, in 1914 and Other Poems, Sidgwick & Jackson, 1915
pair.headnote: Rupert Brooke wrote this sonnet in late 1914, early in the First World War, as the last of a sequence of five war sonnets. He died of illness on the way to Gallipoli in April 1915, before seeing combat.
pair.body:
If I should die, think only this of me:
That there's some corner of a foreign field
That is for ever England. There shall be
In that rich earth a richer dust concealed;
A dust whom England bore, shaped, made aware,
Gave, once, her flowers to love, her ways to roam,
A body of England's, breathing English air,
Washed by the rivers, blest by suns of home.

And think, this heart, all evil shed away,
A pulse in the eternal mind, no less
Gives somewhere back the thoughts by England given;
Her sights and sounds; dreams happy as her day;
And laughter, learnt of friends; and gentleness,
In hearts at peace, under an English heaven.

questions.model: Owen floods the senses so that the reader has to witness the kind of death patriotic rhetoric hides. The attack bursts in as broken exclamations, "Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!", and the capitals and fragments act out the panic, while "An ecstasy of fumbling" is an oxymoron for a frenzy so intense it looks like a fit. Then the visual imagery warps: "Dim, through the misty panes and thick green light, / As under a green sea, I saw him drowning." Through the gas-mask lenses the soldier seems to drown on dry land, and the present participle "drowning" leaves his death unfinished. It comes back in the isolated couplet, "guttering, choking, drowning." In the final stanza Owen moves to sound and texture. We are made to "hear, at every jolt, the blood / Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs", and "Obscene as cancer, bitter as the cud" makes the death disgusting, not noble. All this has a purpose. Once we have seen, heard and nearly tasted that death, Owen can call the patriotic motto what it is: "The old Lie".

questions.model: For Brooke's speaker, dying isn't a loss but a repayment that enriches the place where he falls. "If I should die" accepts death calmly, and he imagines his grave turning "some corner of a foreign field" into ground "That is for ever England." His body will be "a richer dust"; the comparative implies his burial actually improves the foreign soil. Death is framed as giving back what England gave. The nation "bore, shaped, made aware" him, and in the sestet his heart "Gives somewhere back the thoughts by England given." That cycle of receiving and returning makes dying an act of gratitude, and the closing image of "hearts at peace, under an English heaven" presents death as peaceful fulfilment rather than suffering.

questions.model:
Both poems ask us to think about death in war, and they reach opposite conclusions. Brooke idealises dying for England as a peaceful, meaningful gift; Owen exposes that ideal as a lie told to the young.

The soldier's body shows the contrast most clearly. Brooke's speaker addresses a loved reader with calm authority, "If I should die, think only this of me", and imagines his body as "A dust whom England bore, shaped, made aware", purified and absorbed into the nation. Owen's soldiers are "Bent double, like old beggars under sacks", a simile that strips away their youth and heroism, and they march "Drunk with fatigue". Brooke's body is "Washed by the rivers, blest by suns of home"; Owen's men are "blood-shod", all their suffering packed into one grotesque compound word.

Form backs this up. Brooke's sonnet is composed, its regular rhyme and gentle iambic rhythm matching the order of the speaker's faith as it moves smoothly to "hearts at peace, under an English heaven." Owen opens with two stanzas that look like a sonnet's octave and then breaks the pattern. The frantic "Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!" shatters the rhythm, and an isolated couplet, "In all my dreams, before my helpless sight, / He plunges at me, guttering, choking, drowning", shows trauma that won't settle into order.

The sharpest difference is how each poem treats the reader. Brooke's "think only this" limits what we are allowed to imagine and shields civilians from the reality of combat. Owen does the opposite. "If you could hear, at every jolt, the blood / Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs" puts us behind the wagon with the dying man. His bitter address, "My friend, you would not tell with such high zest / To children ardent for some desperate glory, / The old Lie", reads almost like a reply to poems such as Brooke's.

Read together, the poems show how experience shapes representation. Brooke imagines death before the trenches; Owen, writing from them, insists that the dignity of "Dulce et decorum est" can't survive a gas attack.

sets.title: Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802
sets.author: William Wordsworth
sets.source: Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802, in Poems, in Two Volumes, 1807
sets.headnote: William Wordsworth was an English Romantic poet. This Petrarchan sonnet records his view of London from Westminster Bridge early one morning in 1802.
sets.body:
Earth has not anything to show more fair:
Dull would he be of soul who could pass by
A sight so touching in its majesty:
This City now doth, like a garment, wear
The beauty of the morning; silent, bare,
Ships, towers, domes, theatres, and temples lie
Open unto the fields, and to the sky;
All bright and glittering in the smokeless air.
Never did sun more beautifully steep
In his first splendour, valley, rock, or hill;
Ne'er saw I, never felt, a calm so deep!
The river glideth at his own sweet will:
Dear God! the very houses seem asleep;
And all that mighty heart is lying still!

pair.title: London
pair.author: William Blake
pair.source: London, in Songs of Innocence and of Experience, 1794
pair.headnote: William Blake was a London poet, painter and engraver. This poem comes from Songs of Experience; the spelling and punctuation follow his engraved original.
pair.body:
I wander thro' each charter'd street,
Near where the charter'd Thames does flow,
And mark in every face I meet
Marks of weakness, marks of woe.

In every cry of every Man,
In every Infants cry of fear,
In every voice: in every ban,
The mind-forg'd manacles I hear

How the Chimney-sweepers cry
Every blackning Church appalls,
And the hapless Soldiers sigh
Runs in blood down Palace walls

But most thro' midnight streets I hear
How the youthful Harlots curse
Blasts the new-born Infants tear
And blights with plagues the Marriage hearse

The personification and simile show it: the city "doth, like a garment, wear / The beauty of the morning", so London becomes a figure dressed in natural beauty instead of a place of industry. A garment can also be taken off, which hints that the beauty is temporary, put on only for the dawn, and that makes his wonder at seeing it "silent, bare" even stronger.

questions.model: Blake's London suffers everywhere, because of the system, and partly because of what people have accepted. The speaker's walk shows a city that is owned and controlled: "charter'd" describes the streets and even "the charter'd Thames", as if nature itself has been bought and regulated. The pun in "mark in every face I meet / Marks of weakness, marks of woe" turns noticing into branding, as though misery has been stamped on every citizen. In the second stanza the repeated "In every" builds a relentless list that ends in "The mind-forg'd manacles I hear", a metaphor suggesting people are chained by the ideas they accept as much as by the powerful. Blake then ties private misery to public institutions. The "Chimney-sweepers cry" shames the "blackning Church", and the soldier's sigh "Runs in blood down Palace walls", turning a sound into a stain of guilt. The final oxymoron, "Marriage hearse", shows suffering infecting even the start of new life, so there seems to be no escape from it.

questions.model:
Each poem sees London through one speaker, but Wordsworth's city is transcendent and at rest, while Blake's is full of institutional cruelty and human pain.

Wordsworth's speaker stands still above the scene on the bridge, and his opening exaggeration, "Earth has not anything to show more fair", frames the city as a natural wonder. Its "Ships, towers, domes, theatres, and temples" lie "Open unto the fields, and to the sky", so in "the smokeless air" city and nature merge. Blake's speaker walks "thro' each charter'd street" at ground level, and he looks at people, not buildings, finding "Marks of weakness, marks of woe" in every face.

Form and sound reinforce the difference. Wordsworth's Petrarchan sonnet builds to exclamations of wonder, "Dear God! the very houses seem asleep", and its long vowels slow us into the calm he feels. Blake's short quatrains and hammering "every" create a claustrophobic rhythm, and the "blackning Church" and "Palace walls" bring institutions into a city that Wordsworth shows only as architecture.

Most tellingly, Wordsworth's London is beautiful precisely because it is empty and silent: "all that mighty heart is lying still!" Blake's London is defined by human noise, "the youthful Harlots curse" heard through "midnight streets". Read side by side, the poems suggest the idealised city only exists while its people sleep, and Blake insists we listen to them.

sets.title: The Drover's Wife (extract)
sets.author: Henry Lawson
sets.source: The Drover's Wife, in While the Billy Boils, Angus & Robertson, 1896 (first published in The Bulletin, 1892)
sets.headnote: Henry Lawson was an Australian writer of stories and verse about bush life in the 1890s. This is the opening of his short story about a woman left alone with her children on an isolated selection.
sets.body:
The two-roomed house is built of round timber, slabs, and stringy-bark, and floored with split slabs. A big bark kitchen standing at one end is larger than the house itself, veranda included.

Bush all round—bush with no horizon, for the country is flat. No ranges in the distance. The bush consists of stunted, rotten native apple-trees. No undergrowth. Nothing to relieve the eye save the darker green of a few she-oaks which are sighing above the narrow, almost waterless creek. Nineteen miles to the nearest sign of civilization—a shanty on the main road.

The drover, an ex-squatter, is away with sheep. His wife and children are left here alone.

Four ragged, dried-up-looking children are playing about the house. Suddenly one of them yells: 'Snake! Mother, here's a snake!'

The gaunt, sun-browned bushwoman dashes from the kitchen, snatches her baby from the ground, holds it on her left hip, and reaches for a stick.

'Where is it?'

'Here! gone into the wood-heap!' yells the eldest boy—a sharp-faced urchin of eleven. 'Stop there, mother! I'll have him. Stand back! I'll have the beggar!'

'Tommy, come here, or you'll be bit. Come here at once when I tell you, you little wretch!'

The youngster comes reluctantly, carrying a stick bigger than himself. Then he yells, triumphantly: 'There it goes—under the house!' and darts away with club uplifted. At the same time the big, black, yellow-eyed dog-of-all-breeds, who has shown the wildest interest in the proceedings, breaks his chain and rushes after that snake. He is a moment late, however, and his nose reaches the crack in the slabs just as the end of its tail disappears. Almost at the same moment the boy's club comes down and skins the aforesaid nose. Alligator takes small notice of this, and proceeds to undermine the building; but he is subdued after a struggle and chained up. They cannot afford to lose him.

pair.title: The Chosen Vessel (extract)
pair.author: Barbara Baynton
pair.source: The Chosen Vessel, in Bush Studies, Duckworth, 1902
pair.headnote: Barbara Baynton was an Australian writer whose collection Bush Studies presents a darker view of bush life than many writers of her time. This is the opening paragraph of her story about a young mother on a remote selection.
pair.body: She laid the stick and her baby on the grass while she untied the rope that tethered the calf. The length of the rope separated them. The cow was near the calf, and both were lying down. Feed along the creek was plentiful, and every day she found a fresh place to tether it, since tether it she must, for if she did not, it would stray with the cow out on the plain. She had plenty of time to go after it, but then there was baby; and if the cow turned on her out on the plain, and she with baby,—she had been a town girl and was afraid of the cow, but she did not want the cow to know it. She used to run at first when it bellowed its protest against the penning up of its calf. This satisfied the cow, also the calf, but the woman's husband was angry, and called her—the noun was cur. It was he who forced her to run and meet the advancing cow, brandishing a stick, and uttering threatening words till the enemy turned and ran. 'That's the way!' the man said, laughing at her white face. In many things he was worse than the cow, and she wondered if the same rule would apply to the man, but she was not one to provoke skirmishes even with the cow.

questions.model: Lawson makes the setting harsh, monotonous and isolating, so we understand the bushwoman's life as endurance with no one to help. The opening reads like an inventory, "The two-roomed house is built of round timber, slabs, and stringy-bark", and the present tense makes the scene feel permanent. Minor sentences like "No ranges in the distance." and "No undergrowth." build a pattern of negation, defining the land by what it lacks, and there is "no horizon, for the country is flat", an enclosure with no visible way out. Even the trees are "stunted, rotten native apple-trees", words of decay and stunted growth that match the family's poverty, and the she-oaks "sighing above the narrow, almost waterless creek" give the scene a mournful tone. The isolation is measured exactly: "Nineteen miles to the nearest sign of civilization", and that sign turns out to be just "a shanty on the main road", a deflating anticlimax. Against all this, the plain sentence "His wife and children are left here alone" carries real weight. When the snake appears, we know she will face it with only her children and a dog.

questions.model: The marriage Baynton shows runs on contempt and intimidation, and the husband is more dangerous than anything on the land. When the woman runs from the bellowing cow, he is furious and abuses her. The narrator's detached aside, "the noun was cur", holds the insult back until the end of the sentence, so the single word lands like a blow and reduces her to an animal. His mockery is physical as well: he laughs "at her white face", amused by her fear. The narrator's ironic "In many things he was worse than the cow" spells out the threat, and her wondering whether "the same rule would apply to the man" suggests she is always calculating how to handle him. Fear has been folded into everyday routine.

questions.model:
Together the extracts suggest that a bushwoman's life is defined by isolation, constant watchfulness and a strength nobody recognises. Where they differ is in where they find the greatest threat: Lawson in the land, Baynton in the man.

In Text 1 the husband's absence is stated flatly: "The drover, an ex-squatter, is away with sheep. His wife and children are left here alone." "left" hints at abandonment, and when the snake appears the woman acts instantly: she "snatches her baby from the ground, holds it on her left hip, and reaches for a stick." The run of urgent verbs makes her competence look instinctive, a habit hammered in by necessity. Baynton's woman also has a stick and "her baby", but her courage is forced on her. She "had been a town girl and was afraid of the cow", and it is her husband "who forced her to run and meet the advancing cow, brandishing a stick".

The narrative viewpoints differ too. Lawson's present-tense narration is sympathetic but external; she is "The gaunt, sun-browned bushwoman", a description showing how the land has shaped her body. Baynton stays closer to the woman's mind, and her irony is darker. "In many things he was worse than the cow" reveals that the real danger is human. Even fear has to be hidden, since "she did not want the cow to know it", which suggests she has learned to hide weakness from every creature around her, her husband included.

Put together, the extracts complicate the masculine bush legend of the 1890s. Lawson honours the woman's endurance in a hostile environment; Baynton exposes the domestic cruelty the legend ignores. Between them they suggest the bushwoman's courage is real, but that isolation, danger and men demand it of her. She doesn't get to choose it.

sets.title: Clancy of the Overflow
sets.author: A. B. (Banjo) Paterson
sets.source: Clancy of the Overflow, in The Man from Snowy River and Other Verses, Angus & Robertson, 1895 (first published in The Bulletin, 1889)
sets.headnote: A. B. 'Banjo' Paterson was a Sydney solicitor and one of the best-known Australian balladists of the 1890s. In this poem a city office worker imagines the life of a drover he once met. The Overflow is the name of a sheep station.
sets.body:
I had written him a letter which I had, for want of better
Knowledge, sent to where I met him down the Lachlan, years ago,
He was shearing when I knew him, so I sent the letter to him,
Just "on spec", addressed as follows: "Clancy, of The Overflow".

And an answer came directed in a writing unexpected,
(And I think the same was written with a thumbnail dipped in tar)
'Twas his shearing mate who wrote it, and verbatim I will quote it:
"Clancy's gone to Queensland droving, and we don't know where he are."

In my wild erratic fancy visions come to me of Clancy
Gone a-droving "down the Cooper" where the western drovers go;
As the stock are slowly stringing, Clancy rides behind them singing,
For the drover's life has pleasures that the townsfolk never know.

And the bush hath friends to meet him, and their kindly voices greet him
In the murmur of the breezes and the river on its bars,
And he sees the vision splendid of the sunlit plains extended,
And at night the wond'rous glory of the everlasting stars.

I am sitting in my dingy little office, where a stingy
Ray of sunlight struggles feebly down between the houses tall,
And the foetid air and gritty of the dusty, dirty city
Through the open window floating, spreads its foulness over all.

And in place of lowing cattle, I can hear the fiendish rattle
Of the tramways and the buses making hurry down the street,
And the language uninviting of the gutter children fighting,
Comes fitfully and faintly through the ceaseless tramp of feet.

And the hurrying people daunt me, and their pallid faces haunt me
As they shoulder one another in their rush and nervous haste,
With their eager eyes and greedy, and their stunted forms and weedy,
For townsfolk have no time to grow, they have no time to waste.

And I somehow rather fancy that I'd like to change with Clancy,
Like to take a turn at droving where the seasons come and go,
While he faced the round eternal of the cash-book and the journal—
But I doubt he'd suit the office, Clancy, of "The Overflow".

questions.model: Paterson uses internal rhyme and long, rolling lines to make the bush sound musical and the city sound harsh. Each long line rhymes within itself, so the bush stanzas flow like song: "As the stock are slowly stringing, Clancy rides behind them singing". The matched endings and soft s sounds imitate the drover's unhurried, contented pace. Natural sounds are gentle, "the murmur of the breezes and the river on its bars", with soft m and r sounds. In the city stanzas the same devices start to grate. "the foetid air and gritty of the dusty, dirty city" crams hard t and d sounds together, so the line feels as clogged as the air it describes. The "fiendish rattle / Of the tramways and the buses" takes the place of the "lowing cattle", and the rhyme itself acts out machine replacing animal. Even people are just noise, "the ceaseless tramp of feet". By running one musical pattern through both worlds, Paterson makes us hear the bush as harmony and the city as discord.

questions.model:
The poem gives a largely romanticised picture of bush life, but Paterson frames it as a city clerk's fantasy, which lets us see the idealising for what it is.

The romance is obvious in the speaker's imagery. Clancy rides "behind them singing", and "the bush hath friends to meet him", personification that makes the landscape a welcoming companion. The elevated diction of "the vision splendid of the sunlit plains extended" and "the wond'rous glory of the everlasting stars" gives droving an almost spiritual grandeur, and the claim that it offers "pleasures that the townsfolk never know" leaves out drought, isolation and hard work altogether.

Paterson signals, though, that this is imagined. It all comes from the speaker's "wild erratic fancy", and he admits that "visions come to me of Clancy", so the bush we see is a projection of his own discontent. The comic reply from the shearing mate, apparently written "with a thumbnail dipped in tar" and ending "we don't know where he are", gives a glimpse of the real, rough bush and gently undercuts the grand vision.

The ending qualifies the fantasy too. The speaker would "like to change with Clancy", but concludes "I doubt he'd suit the office", a wry admission that the two worlds can't just be swapped. So the poem romanticises the bush to a great extent, but knowingly: the idealising comes as much from the speaker's longing to escape the city as from the bush itself.

sets.title: Bell-Birds
sets.author: Henry Kendall
sets.source: Bell-Birds, in Leaves from Australian Forests, George Robertson, 1869
sets.headnote: Henry Kendall was a colonial Australian poet who grew up on the south coast of New South Wales. This lyric celebrates the bell-bird (bell miner) of the coastal forests.
sets.body:
By channels of coolness the echoes are calling,
And down the dim gorges I hear the creek falling:
It lives in the mountain where moss and the sedges
Touch with their beauty the banks and the ledges.
Through breaks of the cedar and sycamore bowers
Struggles the light that is love to the flowers;
And, softer than slumber, and sweeter than singing,
The notes of the bell-birds are running and ringing.

The silver-voiced bell-birds, the darlings of daytime!
They sing in September their songs of the May-time;
When shadows wax strong, and the thunder-bolts hurtle,
They hide with their fear in the leaves of the myrtle;
When rain and the sunbeams shine mingled together,
They start up like fairies that follow fair weather;
And straightway the hues of their feathers unfolden
Are the green and the purple, the blue and the golden.

October, the maiden of bright yellow tresses,
Loiters for love in these cool wildernesses;
Loiters, knee-deep, in the grasses, to listen,
Where dripping rocks gleam and the leafy pools glisten:
Then is the time when the water-moons splendid
Break with their gold, and are scattered or blended
Over the creeks, till the woodlands have warning
Of songs of the bell-bird and wings of the Morning.

Welcome as waters unkissed by the summers
Are the voices of bell-birds to thirsty far-comers.
When fiery December sets foot in the forest,
And the need of the wayfarer presses the sorest,
Pent in the ridges for ever and ever
The bell-birds direct him to spring and to river,
With ring and with ripple, like runnels whose torrents
Are toned by the pebbles and leaves in the currents.

Often I sit, looking back to a childhood,
Mixt with the sights and the sounds of the wildwood,
Longing for power and the sweetness to fashion,
Lyrics with beats like a heart-beat of passion—
Songs interwoven of lights and of laughters
Borrowed from bell-birds in far forest-rafters;
So I might keep in the city and alleys
The beauty and strength of the deep mountain valleys:
Charming to slumber the pain of my losses
With glimpses of creeks and a vision of mosses.

The abstract noun "coolness" makes the sound itself feel refreshing, and the speaker hears "the creek falling". Sight and touch combine as moss and sedges "Touch with their beauty the banks and the ledges", and the light "Struggles" through "breaks of the cedar", so we picture a shaded, enclosed forest. The stanza builds to "softer than slumber, and sweeter than singing", paired comparatives whose soft s sounds are as gentle as the birdsong. The setting is felt with the whole body: peaceful, musical, and sheltered from the heat outside.

questions.model: Personification fills Kendall's bush with personalities, so the landscape becomes a gentle community. The birds are "the darlings of daytime", an affectionate, alliterative name that makes them cherished. They have feelings, too. In storms "They hide with their fear in the leaves of the myrtle", which makes them vulnerable and endearing, and they "start up like fairies that follow fair weather", a simile borrowed from European fairy tale that turns the Australian forest into an enchanted place. The months get the fullest treatment: "October, the maiden of bright yellow tresses, / Loiters for love in these cool wildernesses". Spring becomes a young beauty who lingers because she loves the place as well. The birds even act as guides, since they "direct him to spring and to river" when "the need of the wayfarer presses the sorest". Through personification the bush stops being a hostile wilderness and becomes a welcoming, protective world that looks after whoever enters it.

questions.model:
The final stanza matters enormously, because it recasts the whole poem as memory and longing. The lush bush of the earlier stanzas turns out to be remembered by a speaker who is now cut off from it.

Up to here the poem is mostly in the present tense. The creek is "falling" and the bell-birds are "running and ringing", so we experience the bush as immediate. Then the perspective shifts: "Often I sit, looking back to a childhood, / Mixt with the sights and the sounds of the wildwood". Suddenly all that sensory richness is reconstructed, and its vividness becomes evidence of how much the speaker misses what he has lost.

The stanza also turns the poem towards poetry itself. He longs for "power and the sweetness to fashion, / Lyrics with beats like a heart-beat of passion", linking poetic rhythm to a pulse. His wish for "Songs interwoven of lights and of laughters / Borrowed from bell-birds" makes the birds the source of his art, and we can read the poem's own lilting rhythm and dense rhyme as the attempt he describes.

Most importantly, the stanza sets bush against city. He hopes he "might keep in the city and alleys / The beauty and strength of the deep mountain valleys", easing "the pain of my losses / With glimpses of creeks and a vision of mosses." "pain" brings in a grief we haven't seen before, and the return to creeks and moss echoes the opening "moss and the sedges". The poem ends where it began, but now the bush is a consolation, not something he is standing in.

Some readers may find the turn sentimental. It is also what gives the poem its emotional depth. The final stanza shows the earlier celebration was a remembered refuge, and it presents poetry as the way to carry the bush into a harsher city life. It isn't just a conclusion; it's the key to the whole poem.

sets.title: Because I could not stop for Death
sets.author: Emily Dickinson
sets.source: Because I could not stop for Death (c. 1862), first published in Poems, 1890; text from the poet's manuscript version
sets.headnote: Emily Dickinson was an American poet who published almost nothing in her lifetime. This poem, written around 1862, imagines death as a carriage ride; the dashes and capital letters are her own.
sets.body:
Because I could not stop for Death –
He kindly stopped for me –
The Carriage held but just Ourselves –
And Immortality.

We slowly drove – He knew no haste
And I had put away
My labor and my leisure too,
For His Civility –

We passed the School, where Children strove
At Recess – in the Ring –
We passed the Fields of Gazing Grain –
We passed the Setting Sun –

Or rather – He passed Us –
The Dews drew quivering and Chill –
For only Gossamer, my Gown –
My Tippet – only Tulle –

We paused before a House that seemed
A Swelling of the Ground –
The Roof was scarcely visible –
The Cornice – in the Ground –

Since then – 'tis Centuries – and yet
Feels shorter than the Day
I first surmised the Horses' Heads
Were toward Eternity –

questions.model:
The poem is a carriage ride through the stages of life to the grave and beyond, so dying becomes a slow, almost unnoticeable journey. The pace is unhurried, "We slowly drove – He knew no haste", and the speaker has "put away / My labor and my leisure too", handing over the whole of her earthly life to Death's courtesy.

The third stanza squeezes a lifetime into three images. With each "We passed" she moves on: the "School, where Children strove" (childhood), the "Fields of Gazing Grain" (maturity and harvest), and "the Setting Sun" (old age, the end of the day). "Gazing" personifies the grain, as if the living world is watching her leave it. Then the journey shifts: "Or rather – He passed Us –". The correction shows she has stopped moving with time. "The Dews drew quivering and Chill" brings the physical cold of death, and her clothes, "only Gossamer, my Gown", seem made for a wedding, not a burial.

The destination is a grave described as a home: "A House that seemed / A Swelling of the Ground", its roof "scarcely visible". The euphemism softens the horror, and the dashes slow us down as the carriage pauses. Finally the timescale collapses. Centuries have passed, yet they feel "shorter than the Day / I first surmised the Horses' Heads / Were toward Eternity". The journey doesn't end at the grave but in an eternity she only understands looking back.

questions.model:
For the most part the poem refuses to make death frightening, turning it into a courteous companion. Details of cold, exposure and confinement, though, carry an unease that complicates the speaker's calm.

The main tone is serene. Death "kindly stopped for me", and her readiness to put aside her "labor" and "leisure" "For His Civility" suggests she accepts as if it were a social call. The steady alternation of longer and shorter lines, close to hymn metre, gives the poem a measured pace that matches "He knew no haste". The grave is softened into "a House" that is just "A Swelling of the Ground", homely rather than morbid. Nothing in the first half asks us to flinch; the horror we might expect has been replaced by good manners.

Underneath, the poem quietly unsettles that composure. "Or rather – He passed Us –" shows she has dropped out of time, which is disorienting, and "The Dews drew quivering and Chill" makes her physically vulnerable; "quivering" suggests fear as well as cold. Her clothes, "only Gossamer, my Gown" and "My Tippet – only Tulle", show she isn't prepared, and the repeated "only" registers a growing sense of exposure. The roof "scarcely visible" and the "Cornice – in the Ground" hint at burial and enclosure.

The final stanza holds both readings. Centuries have passed in death, yet they feel "shorter than the Day / I first surmised the Horses' Heads / Were toward Eternity". "surmised" suggests a dawning and perhaps unsettling realisation: the polite drive had a destination she didn't choose. The closing dash leaves the poem unresolved, not triumphant.

So death is presented as something to accept rather than fear, but Dickinson runs a thread of unease under the courtesy, and we sense the shock the speaker's composure is hiding.

sets.author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
sets.source: God's Grandeur (written 1877), in Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins (ed. Robert Bridges), Humphrey Milford, 1918
sets.headnote: Gerard Manley Hopkins was an English poet and Jesuit priest. This Petrarchan sonnet, written in 1877 and published after his death, responds to the industrial landscape of Victorian Britain.

questions.model: Hopkins first uses repetition to make human activity sound relentless and mechanical: "Generations have trod, have trod, have trod". Saying it three times imitates the tread of feet over centuries, wearing the earth down. He then packs in internal rhyme: "And all is seared with trade; bleared, smeared with toil". The cluster of "seared", "bleared" and "smeared" sounds harsh and cluttered, like the grime of industry, as if commerce and labour have burned and blurred the world. Together the techniques present the damage as built up over time and spread everywhere, ending in a foot that can't feel the soil, "being shod", cut off from the nature it has spoiled.

questions.model: In the sestet despair gives way to hope, as Hopkins insists that nature's divine source can't be used up. The volta comes at "And for all this, nature is never spent", and the absolute "never" answers everything the octave listed. Hopkins puts renewal under the surface: "There lives the dearest freshness deep down things", where "dearest" and "deep down" stress a vitality that is hidden but lasting. Sunset and sunrise act out that renewal: "though the last lights off the black West went / Oh, morning, at the brown brink eastward, springs". The exclamation and the delayed verb "springs" make dawn burst out after a long stretch of dark. Finally the source of hope is named. The Holy Ghost "over the bent / World broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings." The enjambment bends "World" over the line, and the image of a bird brooding on its nest makes God tenderly protective of creation, while "ah!" catches the speaker's wonder.

questions.model:
Hopkins's sound does real work. He makes us hear the argument: the energy of God's presence, the dead weight of human toil, and the renewing power of the Holy Ghost.

The opening lines use sound for divine energy. The world "will flame out, like shining from shook foil", and "shining" and "shook" flash like shaken metal. The next image works differently: "It gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil / Crushed." The long vowels slow the line down, and the heavy stress on "Crushed" after the line break acts out pressure building and then releasing.

Then sound carries the damage. "have trod, have trod, have trod" is a dull, plodding beat, while the internal rhymes "seared", "bleared" and "smeared" and the paired "wears man's smudge and shares man's smell" crowd the lines with hissing and echoes, so the language itself feels dirty.

In the sestet the sound softens. "deep down things" and the breathy "warm breast" and "bright wings" sound warm and tender, enacting the comfort they describe. Some readers will find the density of sound overwhelming or obscure. That difficulty is part of why it works, though: Hopkins forces slow, careful reading, which mirrors the attention to nature the poem asks for. The sound isn't decoration. It is how we feel the poem's ideas.

sets.title: Ozymandias
sets.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
sets.source: Ozymandias, first published in The Examiner, 1818; collected in Rosalind and Helen, 1819
sets.headnote: Percy Bysshe Shelley was an English Romantic poet with radical political views. Ozymandias is a Greek name for the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II.
sets.body:
I met a traveller from an antique land,
Who said—"Two vast and trunkless legs of stone
Stand in the desert... Near them, on the sand,
Half sunk a shattered visage lies, whose frown,
And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command,
Tell that its sculptor well those passions read
Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things,
The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed;
And on the pedestal, these words appear:
My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings;
Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare
The lone and level sands stretch far away."

questions.model: Shelley uses situational irony to show that political power, however absolute it claims to be, doesn't last. The central irony is the inscription: "My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; / Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!" The king meant rival rulers to despair at his achievements. Now the command invites a different despair, at how pointless that kind of ambition is, because "Nothing beside remains." That blunt half-line comes straight after the boast and punctures it. The setting adds to the irony: "boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away". The alliteration and long vowels make the desert seem endless, the real eternal power that has swallowed the empire. Even the statue is ironic. What survives isn't the king's greatness but the sculptor's record of his "sneer of cold command", and "the hand that mocked them" has outlasted the ruler. Through irony, Shelley suggests that art and time endure while tyranny ends up a "colossal Wreck".

questions.model:
The layered narration and the irregular sonnet form are central to the poem's meaning. Both keep Ozymandias at a distance from us, and both act out the decay of his power.

The story reaches us through several voices. The speaker says "I met a traveller from an antique land"; the traveller describes the statue; the sculptor interpreted the king; and only then does the inscription speak in the king's own voice. His words come to us fourth-hand, buried at the centre of the poem like the statue in the sand. That matters. The king who ordered others to "Look on my Works" is now known only through a traveller's story and an artist's interpretation, so the framing itself shows how little control he has over his legacy.

The sonnet form is used ironically. Sonnets traditionally celebrate love or promise their subject immortality; Shelley's records a ruler's failed bid for immortality. The form is irregular as well. The rhyme scheme is neither strictly Petrarchan nor Shakespearean, and the turn arrives mid-line at "Nothing beside remains", after the inscription, rather than at a clean break. That instability can be read as a formal echo of the "shattered visage": recognisable, but broken.

In the final lines form and meaning work together. The caesura before "Nothing beside remains" leaves a stark silence after the boast, and "The lone and level sands stretch far away", with its alliteration and slow, heavy stresses, stretches out the way the desert does. We're left with emptiness rather than grandeur.

You could argue the poem's power comes mainly from its central image. But the image depends on the framing. Without the distancing voices and the broken sonnet, the statue would just be a description, not a meditation on time. Framing and form make the decisive contribution, turning a traveller's anecdote into a lasting judgement on tyranny.

sets.title: To Autumn
sets.author: John Keats
sets.source: To Autumn (written September 1819), in Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems, 1820
sets.headnote: John Keats was an English Romantic poet who died of tuberculosis in 1821, aged twenty-five. He wrote this ode in September 1819 after a walk near Winchester.
sets.body:
Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness,
Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun;
Conspiring with him how to load and bless
With fruit the vines that round the thatch-eves run;
To bend with apples the moss'd cottage-trees,
And fill all fruit with ripeness to the core;
To swell the gourd, and plump the hazel shells
With a sweet kernel; to set budding more,
And still more, later flowers for the bees,
Until they think warm days will never cease,
For Summer has o'er-brimm'd their clammy cells.

Who hath not seen thee oft amid thy store?
Sometimes whoever seeks abroad may find
Thee sitting careless on a granary floor,
Thy hair soft-lifted by the winnowing wind;
Or on a half-reap'd furrow sound asleep,
Drows'd with the fume of poppies, while thy hook
Spares the next swath and all its twined flowers:
And sometimes like a gleaner thou dost keep
Steady thy laden head across a brook;
Or by a cyder-press, with patient look,
Thou watchest the last oozings hours by hours.

Where are the songs of Spring? Ay, where are they?
Think not of them, thou hast thy music too,—
While barred clouds bloom the soft-dying day,
And touch the stubble-plains with rosy hue;
Then in a wailful choir the small gnats mourn
Among the river sallows, borne aloft
Or sinking as the light wind lives or dies;
And full-grown lambs loud bleat from hilly bourn;
Hedge-crickets sing; and now with treble soft
The red-breast whistles from a garden-croft;
And gathering swallows twitter in the skies.

Autumn is the "Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun", "Conspiring with him how to load and bless / With fruit the vines", so ripeness comes out of an intimate partnership. The stanza ends in excess: summer "has o'er-brimm'd their clammy cells", the honeycomb spilling over. The bees "think warm days will never cease", which hints that the plenty can't last, but what we're left with is richness.

questions.model:
In the second stanza autumn becomes a series of farm workers, each caught in a moment of drowsy stillness, so the season is a human presence resting in the middle of the harvest.

"Who hath not seen thee oft amid thy store?" assumes we already know this figure, and invites us to see autumn everywhere. First it is "sitting careless on a granary floor, / Thy hair soft-lifted by the winnowing wind". The soft w sounds and the lifted hair make the figure relaxed, almost weightless, as if the breeze is doing the work of separating grain from chaff. Next, autumn lies "on a half-reap'd furrow sound asleep, / Drows'd with the fume of poppies", while the hook "Spares the next swath and all its twined flowers". The reaping is unfinished, so the harvest, and time itself, seems paused, and sparing the flowers suggests mercy.

The gleaner must "keep / Steady thy laden head across a brook", and the line break between "keep" and "Steady" mimics the act of holding still. Finally, by the cider-press, autumn watches "with patient look" over "the last oozings hours by hours." The slow "hours by hours" stretches time out, while "last" gives us the first hint of an ending.

Through these portraits Keats turns autumn from an abstract season into a calm, patient presence whose stillness holds time in balance, just for a while.

questions.model:
Over its three stanzas the poem moves from ripening to harvest to aftermath, and from morning to evening. Through that progression Keats responds to time passing with neither denial nor grief, but with acceptance of the beauty in things that don't last.

The first stanza is all growth. Its sprawling sentence piles up infinitives, "To swell the gourd, and plump the hazel shells", so ripening seems ongoing and unstoppable. Time is there even so. The bees "think warm days will never cease", an illusion we can see through, and the honeycomb is "o'er-brimm'd", ripeness right at the point of excess.

The second stanza slows time almost to a stop. Autumn lies "sound asleep" on a "half-reap'd furrow", and the figure at the cider-press watches "the last oozings hours by hours". The season hangs between fullness and completion. The work isn't finished, but "last" tells us the harvest is ending.

The third stanza faces loss head-on, "Where are the songs of Spring? Ay, where are they?", and immediately redirects the question: "Think not of them, thou hast thy music too". Its images are of ending, "the soft-dying day" and the "stubble-plains", and of uncertainty, with the gnats "borne aloft / Or sinking as the light wind lives or dies". The "wailful choir" mourns, but it is balanced by signs of life: lambs "bleat", "Hedge-crickets sing", and "gathering swallows twitter in the skies", birds getting ready to migrate.

Taken as a whole, the stanzas make one movement from abundance to departure, and Keats's response comes out of that shape. Instead of mourning spring or clinging to summer, the poem finds the music that belongs to each stage of decline. The gathering swallows suggest an ending and a continuation somewhere else at once, so the poem accepts that time passing can't be separated from the fullness it celebrates.

sets.title: Remember
sets.author: Christina Rossetti
sets.source: Remember (written 1849), in Goblin Market and Other Poems, Macmillan, 1862
sets.headnote: Christina Rossetti was an English Victorian poet. In this Petrarchan sonnet a speaker addresses a loved one about how she wishes to be remembered after her death.
sets.body:
Remember me when I am gone away,
Gone far away into the silent land;
When you can no more hold me by the hand,
Nor I half turn to go yet turning stay.
Remember me when no more day by day
You tell me of our future that you planned:
Only remember me; you understand
It will be late to counsel then or pray.
Yet if you should forget me for a while
And afterwards remember, do not grieve:
For if the darkness and corruption leave
A vestige of the thoughts that once I had,
Better by far you should forget and smile
Than that you should remember and be sad.

The octave is dominated by "Remember me", but the sestet opens with "Yet", a concession that reverses the argument: "Yet if you should forget me for a while / And afterwards remember, do not grieve". Now she permits forgetting, and the new command, "do not grieve", replaces the old demand. Her reason comes through the stark phrase "the darkness and corruption", a frank image of death and decay that is far harsher than the gentle "silent land" of line 2. If death leaves only "A vestige of the thoughts that once I had", she would rather spare her beloved the pain of that memory. The closing antithesis makes her priority clear: "Better by far you should forget and smile / Than that you should remember and be sad." Setting "forget and smile" against "remember and be sad" shows her love has shifted from wanting to be remembered to wanting her beloved to be happy.

questions.model:
The Petrarchan sonnet suits this poem extremely well. Splitting it into octave and sestet lets Rossetti dramatise a change of heart, so a conventional love poem becomes a meditation on selfless love.

The octave's interlocking rhymes and repeated commands create a closed-in, insistent voice. "Remember me" keeps returning, and the images of a shared life, the beloved who would "hold me by the hand" and talk of "our future", are presented as things about to be lost. Her reluctance to leave, "Nor I half turn to go yet turning stay", is acted out by the line's own turning back on itself.

The volta at "Yet" uses the form's built-in expectation of a turn. Instead of intensifying the plea, Rossetti reverses it, so the sestet answers the octave: the demand to remember becomes permission to forget, and the new rhyme sounds mark the change of thought.

Love sonnets often try to possess the beloved or make them immortal. Rossetti turns that around, because her speaker finally gives up her claim on being remembered. The final lines, "Better by far you should forget and smile / Than that you should remember and be sad", have the balance of a closing couplet and resolve the tension through clear antithesis.

You could argue the form is restrictive and the shift too sudden. But the compression is part of the effect. In fourteen lines the speaker moves from need to generosity, and the strict structure makes that movement visible. The form isn't just a container; it's how the poem shows her emotional growth.

sets.title: The Darkling Thrush
sets.author: Thomas Hardy
sets.source: The Darkling Thrush (dated 31 December 1900), in Poems of the Past and the Present, Harper & Brothers, 1901
sets.headnote: Thomas Hardy was an English novelist and poet. He dated this poem 31 December 1900, the last day of the nineteenth century. 'Darkling' means in the dark or growing dark.
sets.body:
I leant upon a coppice gate
When Frost was spectre-grey,
And Winter's dregs made desolate
The weakening eye of day.
The tangled bine-stems scored the sky
Like strings of broken lyres,
And all mankind that haunted nigh
Had sought their household fires.

The land's sharp features seemed to be
The Century's corpse outleant,
His crypt the cloudy canopy,
The wind his death-lament.
The ancient pulse of germ and birth
Was shrunken hard and dry,
And every spirit upon earth
Seemed fervourless as I.

At once a voice arose among
The bleak twigs overhead
In a full-hearted evensong
Of joy illimited;
An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small,
In blast-beruffled plume,
Had chosen thus to fling his soul
Upon the growing gloom.

So little cause for carolings
Of such ecstatic sound
Was written on terrestrial things
Afar or nigh around,
That I could think there trembled through
His happy good-night air
Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew
And I was unaware.

"dregs" suggests the worthless leftovers of the season, and the sun becomes a dimming eye. "Like strings of broken lyres" turns the bare stems into ruined instruments, as if music and joy have been silenced. In the second stanza the landscape becomes "The Century's corpse outleant", with the sky as "His crypt" and the wind as "his death-lament", an extended metaphor that turns the end of the century into a funeral. And the speaker shares the deadness: every spirit "Seemed fervourless as I". The desolation is inside him as much as outside.

questions.model: The thrush is an unlikely source of joy, and its song defies everything around it. The voice arrives suddenly, "At once", and setting "The bleak twigs overhead" against "a full-hearted evensong / Of joy illimited" pits limitless joy against a barren scene. "evensong", an evening church service, gives the song a religious quality, as if the bird were worshipping. Yet the bird itself is unimpressive: "An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small", a list of short adjectives that stresses how fragile it is, and its "blast-beruffled plume" suggests feathers battered by the wind. That makes its choice to "fling his soul / Upon the growing gloom" all the more striking. "fling" is reckless and wholehearted, and the alliteration in "growing gloom" reminds us of the dark the song is pushing against. The thrush becomes a figure of courageous hope, and its smallness makes its defiance even bigger.

questions.model:
The poem offers a fragile, uncertain hope for the new century. The thrush's song suggests hope exists, but the speaker can't share it, and Hardy's careful wording keeps that hope at arm's length.

The first half leaves little room for optimism. Dated on the last day of 1900, the poem imagines the landscape as "The Century's corpse outleant" and declares that "The ancient pulse of germ and birth / Was shrunken hard and dry". If nature's cycle of renewal has shrunk, this is more than winter; an entire age seems exhausted, and the speaker himself is "fervourless".

The thrush seems to overturn all this. Its "full-hearted evensong / Of joy illimited" brings unexpected energy, and its decision to "fling his soul / Upon the growing gloom" makes hope an act of will rather than a reaction to circumstances. Because the bird is "aged" and "frail", hope seems able to survive even in a weakened state; perhaps the old century can hand something on to the new one.

The final stanza qualifies that hope, though. The speaker stresses there was "So little cause for carolings / Of such ecstatic sound", admitting that nothing he can see justifies the song. All he can say is that "I could think there trembled through / His happy good-night air / Some blessed Hope". The conditional "could think" and the vague "Some" make the hope tentative, and "trembled" makes it fragile. Above all, the closing lines admit this was a Hope "whereof he knew / And I was unaware." The speaker stays outside it.

So hope is present but not possessed. Hardy suggests the new century might hold reasons for joy, but his sceptical speaker can't reach them, and we're left with a hope that is real but unconfirmed.

sets.title: Break of Day in the Trenches
sets.author: Isaac Rosenberg
sets.source: Break of Day in the Trenches, first published in Poetry (Chicago), December 1916
sets.headnote: Isaac Rosenberg was an English poet and painter who served as a private on the Western Front and was killed in April 1918. He wrote this poem in the trenches in 1916.
sets.body:
The darkness crumbles away.
It is the same old druid Time as ever,
Only a live thing leaps my hand,
A queer sardonic rat,
As I pull the parapet's poppy
To stick behind my ear.
Droll rat, they would shoot you if they knew
Your cosmopolitan sympathies.
Now you have touched this English hand
You will do the same to a German
Soon, no doubt, if it be your pleasure
To cross the sleeping green between.
It seems you inwardly grin as you pass
Strong eyes, fine limbs, haughty athletes,
Less chanced than you for life,
Bonds to the whims of murder,
Sprawled in the bowels of the earth,
The torn fields of France.
What do you see in our eyes
At the shrieking iron and flame
Hurled through still heavens?
What quaver—what heart aghast?
Poppies whose roots are in man's veins
Drop, and are ever dropping;
But mine in my ear is safe—
Just a little white with the dust.

It's "A queer sardonic rat", as if it's mocking the war, and the speaker jokes that "they would shoot you if they knew / Your cosmopolitan sympathies". Having "touched this English hand", it will "do the same to a German", so the rat shows how absurd a national hatred is when an animal can simply ignore it.

questions.model:
The poppy frames the poem. It links the speaker's own fragile survival to the deaths of countless soldiers, and quietly reworks a familiar image of beauty and remembrance.

It first appears as a casual gesture: the speaker pulls "the parapet's poppy / To stick behind my ear." It's almost playful, a soldier decorating himself. But the flower grows on the parapet, the edge of the trench where men are most exposed, so beauty and danger sit side by side.

Its full meaning comes near the end: "Poppies whose roots are in man's veins / Drop, and are ever dropping". If the roots draw on human blood, the flowers are growing out of the dead, and the red poppy becomes an image of bloodshed feeding the earth. "Drop" and the continuous "ever dropping" suggest falling petals and falling soldiers, a loss that keeps happening.

The last lines return to the speaker's own flower: "But mine in my ear is safe— / Just a little white with the dust." Setting "mine" against the endlessly dropping poppies marks the speaker out as spared for now, but "Just" and the whitening flower undercut that safety. The white drains away the poppy's colour, suggesting pallor and death, and dust recalls burial.

Through the poppy, Rosenberg presents death in war as natural, cyclical and indiscriminate, and survival as precarious and temporary, nothing heroic about it.

questions.model:
Rosenberg's tone is ironic, understated and quietly appalled, and it shapes everything about how the poem represents war. It exposes the absurdity and waste of the conflict without heroic rhetoric and without open outrage.

The opening voice is calm, almost chatty. "The darkness crumbles away" describes dawn in the trenches without any drama, and "It is the same old druid Time as ever" suggests weariness, as if war were just another episode in ancient, indifferent time. The understatement is unsettling, because the speaker's routine tone sits so oddly against the violence the setting implies.

Talking to the rat brings in a wry irony. He calls it "Droll rat" and notes that "they would shoot you if they knew / Your cosmopolitan sympathies." Behind the joke is a serious point: national hatred is so total that even a rat's indifference to sides looks like treason. The irony deepens as the rat seems to "inwardly grin" at "Strong eyes, fine limbs, haughty athletes, / Less chanced than you for life". The list of the soldiers' physical virtues is undercut by the bitter recognition that a rat has better odds of surviving.

Then the tone darkens. "What do you see in our eyes / At the shrieking iron and flame / Hurled through still heavens?" The "shrieking iron" tears through the "still heavens", and the broken question "What quaver—what heart aghast?" shows a fear the speaker can't fully put into words.

At the end the tone returns to understatement, with the poppy that is "Just a little white with the dust." That restraint is more chilling than any open lament would be.

Some readers may find the restraint detached. In fact it is what gives the poem its force. By refusing patriotic grandeur and avoiding melodrama, Rosenberg shows war as absurd, indiscriminate and quietly devastating, and leaves the reader to supply the outrage the speaker holds back.

sets.title: An Irish Airman Foresees His Death
sets.author: W. B. Yeats
sets.source: An Irish Airman Foresees His Death, in The Wild Swans at Coole, Macmillan, 1919
sets.headnote: W. B. Yeats was an Irish poet. This poem is spoken in the voice of Major Robert Gregory, the son of Yeats's friend Lady Gregory, an Irish pilot in the British air service who was killed in Italy in 1918. Kiltartan is a district near the Gregory family's estate in the west of Ireland.
sets.body:
I know that I shall meet my fate
Somewhere among the clouds above;
Those that I fight I do not hate,
Those that I guard I do not love;
My country is Kiltartan Cross,
My countrymen Kiltartan's poor,
No likely end could bring them loss
Or leave them happier than before.
Nor law, nor duty bade me fight,
Nor public men, nor cheering crowds,
A lonely impulse of delight
Drove to this tumult in the clouds;
I balanced all, brought all to mind,
The years to come seemed waste of breath,
A waste of breath the years behind
In balance with this life, this death.

His real community is local: "My country is Kiltartan Cross, / My countrymen Kiltartan's poor", and he believes no outcome of the war could "bring them loss / Or leave them happier than before." questions.model: Through tightly balanced syntax and a regular form, Yeats shows a mind that has calmly weighed life against death and found them equal. The poem is a single sixteen-line stanza in steady iambic tetrameter with alternating rhyme, and that regularity suggests composure, not fear. Inside the lines, parallelism creates symmetry: "Those that I fight I do not hate, / Those that I guard I do not love". He lists the motives he rejects one after another, "Nor law, nor duty bade me fight, / Nor public men, nor cheering crowds", dismissing each of the usual reasons for going to war. Instead, "A lonely impulse of delight / Drove to this tumult in the clouds"; "delight" against "tumult" captures exhilaration in the middle of danger. The final lines form a chiasmus: "The years to come seemed waste of breath, / A waste of breath the years behind". The mirrored phrasing acts out the weighing, and the last line, "In balance with this life, this death", sets life and death side by side as equal weights. The structure mirrors his detached, deliberate acceptance of his fate.

questions.model:
The airman's death is dignified and freely chosen, but it isn't heroic in the traditional, patriotic sense. Yeats deliberately strips away the motives that normally make a war death heroic.

Conventional heroism rests on loyalty and duty, and the airman rejects both outright: "Nor law, nor duty bade me fight, / Nor public men, nor cheering crowds". Dismissing the "cheering crowds" turns down the public glory wartime propaganda promised. He isn't even fighting for his own nation, since "No likely end could bring them loss / Or leave them happier than before." His death will change nothing for the people he loves.

What's left is a private motive: "A lonely impulse of delight / Drove to this tumult in the clouds." "lonely" isolates the decision, and "delight" suggests exhilaration, not sacrifice. Some readers will see this as a self-absorbed, even nihilistic choice, especially since he writes off both past and future as "waste of breath".

Yet the poem also gives him a kind of heroism: clarity. "I know that I shall meet my fate" is calm and certain, and "I balanced all, brought all to mind" presents a man who has reasoned his way to his choice. The final line, "In balance with this life, this death", gives his death the poise of something chosen with full awareness.

So the poem doesn't celebrate heroism as courage for a cause. It redefines it as the composure of a man who faces death on his own terms.
